question: A 66-year-old man, previously diagnosed with liver cirrhosis of alcoholic etiology, is brought to the Emergency Department due to an increase in the abdominal perimeter and temporo-spatial disorientation. On physical examination, there is evidence of ascites and "flapping tremor" or asterixis. Which of the following explorations should be done as a matter of urgency?

options.opa: A cranial computed tomography to rule out a cerebrovascular accident.
options.opb: An abdominal ultrasound to confirm the presence of ascites.
options.opc: An exploratory paracentesis to rule out a spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
options.opd: An electroencephalogram to confirm the existence of hepatic encephalopathy.
options.ope: An abdominal computed tomography to rule out a hepatocellular carcinoma.

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Ascites in a patient with liver cirrhosis -> high suspicion of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis -> exploratory paracentesis needed. -> 95%
CHAIN: Flapping tremor or asterixis on physical exam -> high suspicion of hepatic encephalopathy -> consider electroencephalogram. -> 90%
CHAIN: Abdominal ultrasound showing ascites -> confirmatory for fluid accumulation in the abdomen. -> 85%
enhanced_information: In a patient with liver cirrhosis presenting with ascites and hepatic encephalopathy symptoms like flapping tremor, the urgent exploration should be an exploratory paracentesis to rule out spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. This is crucial due to the high risk of infection in these patients.
